claim: Eye opening coincides with a sharp decrease in the strength of unitary inhibitory postsynaptic currents (uIPSCs) from somatostatin-expressing interneurons (Sst-INs) to nearby excitatory neurons in layer 2/3 of the mouse visual cortex.
source: Here, we show that coinciding with eye opening, the strength of unitary inhibitory postsynaptic currents (uIPSCs) from somatostatin-expressing interneurons (Sst-INs) to nearby excitatory neurons, but not interneurons, sharply decreases in layer 2/3 of the mouse visual cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing a ~65% reduction in the peak amplitude of uIPSCs from P12-13 to P14-15, as shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Eye opening does not affect the strength of uIPSCs from Sst-INs to interneurons in layer 2/3 of the mouse visual cortex.
source: Here, we show that coinciding with eye opening, the strength of unitary inhibitory postsynaptic currents (uIPSCs) from somatostatin-expressing interneurons (Sst-INs) to nearby excitatory neurons, but not interneurons, sharply decreases in layer 2/3 of the mouse visual cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant changes in Sst-IN→FS-IN and Sst-IN→Htr3a-IN uIPSCs during eye opening, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: The strength of uIPSCs from fast-spiking interneurons (FS-INs) to excitatory neurons significantly increases during eye opening.
source: In contrast, the strength of uIPSCs from fast-spiking interneurons (FS-INs) to excitatory neurons significantly increases during eye opening.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing a ~140% increase in FS-IN→PC uIPSC amplitude from P12-13 to P14-15, as shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Dark rearing prevents the developmental changes in Sst-IN→PC and FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission that occur during eye opening.
source: More importantly, these developmental changes can be prevented by dark rearing or binocular lid suture, and reproduced by the artificial opening of sutured lids.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant changes in Sst-IN→PC uIPSC amplitude between P12-13 and P14-15 in dark-reared mice, as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Binocular lid suture prevents the developmental changes in Sst-IN→PC and FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission that occur during eye opening.
source: More importantly, these developmental changes can be prevented by dark rearing or binocular lid suture, and reproduced by the artificial opening of sutured lids.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant changes in synaptic transmission in continuously sutured mice, as shown in Figure 6.

claim: Artificial opening of sutured lids reproduces the developmental changes in Sst-IN→PC and FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission.
source: More importantly, these developmental changes can be prevented by dark rearing or binocular lid suture, and reproduced by the artificial opening of sutured lids.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that artificially eye-opened mice exhibit decreased Sst-IN→PC and increased FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission, as shown in Figure 6.

claim: The differential maturation of synaptic transmission from Sst-INs and FS-INs to PCs is accompanied by a significant change in the postsynaptic quantal size.
source: Mechanistically, this differential maturation of synaptic transmission is accompanied by a significant change in the postsynaptic quantal size.
evidence: The claim is supported by variance-mean analysis showing that postsynaptic quantal size (Q) decreases in Sst-IN→PC connections and increases in FS-IN→PC connections during eye opening, as shown in Figure 7H and 7P.

claim: Sensory experience critically influences neuronal connectivity and synaptic transmission during neocortical development.
source: During neocortical development, sensory experience critically inﬂuences neuronal connectivity and synaptic transmission (Katz and Shatz, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Katz and Shatz, 1996.

claim: Maturation of the visual cortex depends on visual afferent activity.
source: In the visual system, maturation of the visual cortex depends on visual afferent activity (Hensch, 2005; Hofer et al., 2009; Pecka et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hensch, 2005; Hofer et al., 2009; Pecka et al., 2014.

claim: Eye opening in rodents typically occurs over a short period of one to two days.
source: Eye opening in rodents typically occurs over a short period of one to two days (Gandhi et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gandhi et al., 2005.

claim: Eye opening drives a rapid series of changes in neuronal activity, protein trafficking, synaptogenesis, synaptic receptor composition, and synaptic transmission and plasticity.
source: When experimentally synchronized, eye opening drives a rapid series of changes in neuronal activity, protein trafficking, synaptogenesis, synaptic receptor composition, and synaptic transmission and plasticity (Lu and Constantine-Paton, 2004; Yoshii et al., 2003; Zhao et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lu and Constantine-Paton, 2004; Yoshii et al., 2003; Zhao et al., 2006.

claim: Eye opening affects neuronal circuit development in the retina, superior colliculus, lateral geniculate nucleus, and visual cortex.
source: Moreover, eye opening affects neuronal circuit development in the ascending retinothalamo-cortical pathway at every level: the retina (Feller, 2003; Tian and Copenhagen, 2003), superior colliculus (SC) (Zhao et al., 2006), lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) (Hooks and Chen, 2006; Levitt et al., 2001), and visual cortex (Hoy and Niell, 2015; Ko et al., 2013; Pecka et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies examining different levels of the visual pathway.

claim: The probability and strength of excitatory connections between layer 2/3 pyramidal cells in the visual cortex significantly increased after eye opening.
source: For example, the probability and strength of excitatory connections between layer 2/3 pyramidal cells (PCs) in the visual cortex significantly increased after eye opening, and these changes were prevented by dark rearing (Ishikawa et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ishikawa et al., 2014.

claim: Orientation tuning preferences of fast-spiking interneurons were dependent on normal visual experience after eye opening.
source: Although previous study reported that orientation tuning preferences of fast-spiking interneurons (FS-INs) were dependent on normal visual experience after eye opening (Kuhlman et al., 2011), whether eye opening shapes inhibitory synaptic transmission in the neocortex during development remains unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kuhlman et al., 2011.

claim: GABAergic INs in the mature neocortex can be categorized into three main populations based on the expression of parvalbumin, somatostatin, and the ionotropic serotonin receptor.
source: In the mature neocortex, GABAergic INs can be categorized into three main populations based on the expression of the calcium-binding protein parvalbumin (PV), the neuropeptide somatostatin (Sst), and the ionotropic serotonin receptor (Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2010.

claim: Sst-expressing INs comprise approximately 20-30% of all neocortical INs.
source: Sst-expressing INs (Sst-INs), comprising approximately 20 ~ 30% of all neocortical INs, are among the most prominent GABAergic IN subtypes in the neocortex (Lee et al., 2010; Pfeffer et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2010; Pfeffer et al., 2013.

claim: Sst expression in the superficial neocortex has typically been associated with Martinotti cells.
source: Sst expression in the superficial neocortex has typically been associated with Martinotti cells (MCs)—GABAergic INs with ascending axons that arborize in cortical layer one and spread horizontally to neighboring columns (Fino and Yuste, 2011; Ma et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fino and Yuste, 2011; Ma et al., 2006.

claim: A large fraction of Sst-INs preferentially target distal dendrites of PCs.
source: A large fraction of Sst-INs preferentially target distal dendrites of PCs (Di Cristo et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Di Cristo et al., 2004.

claim: Cortical Sst-INs precisely control the efficacy and plasticity of glutamatergic inputs by regulating postsynaptic spine Ca2+ signals, synaptic dynamics, dendritic spike bursts, and transformation of dendritic inputs.
source: In addition to providing lateral inhibition to local PC networks, cortical Sst-INs also precisely control the efficacy and plasticity of glutamatergic inputs by regulating postsynaptic spine Ca2+ signals, synaptic dynamics, dendritic spike bursts, and transformation of dendritic inputs (Chiu et al., 2013; Higley, 2014; Lovett-Barron et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chiu et al., 2013; Higley, 2014; Lovett-Barron et al., 2012.

claim: Cortical Sst-INs frequently inhibit other cortical INs (disinhibition).
source: Furthermore, cortical Sst-INs not only innervate PCs but also frequently inhibit other cortical INs (disinhibition) (Pfeffer et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pfeffer et al., 2013.

claim: PV-expressing FS-INs constitute ~40% of cortical GABAergic neurons.
source: PV-expressing FS-INs, which constitute ~40% of cortical GABAergic neurons, form powerful synapses onto the somatic and perisomatic compartments of PCs (Di Cristo et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Di Cristo et al., 2004.

claim: PV-expressing FS-INs form powerful synapses onto the somatic and perisomatic compartments of PCs.
source: PV-expressing FS-INs, which constitute ~40% of cortical GABAergic neurons, form powerful synapses onto the somatic and perisomatic compartments of PCs (Di Cristo et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Di Cristo et al., 2004.

claim: The emergence and maturation of connections from PV-INs to PCs and PV-INs have been reported previously.
source: Although the emergence and maturation of connections from PV-INs to PCs and PV-INs have been reported previously (Lazarus and Huang, 2011); Pangratz-Fuehrer and Hestrin, 2011); Yang et al., 2014), the development of inhibitory synaptic transmission (including amplitude and connectivity) from Sst-INs to PCs and other IN subtypes remains largely unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lazarus and Huang, 2011; Pangratz-Fuehrer and Hestrin, 2011; Yang et al., 2014.

claim: Sst-INs regulate learning-induced and experience-dependent cortical plasticity through feedforward as well as feedback inhibitions, both during early postnatal development and in adulthood.
source: In addition, accumulating evidence indicates that Sst-INs regulate learning-induced and experience-dependent cortical plasticity through feedforward as well as feedback inhibitions, both during early postnatal development and in adulthood (Bloodgood et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2015; Marques-Smith et al., 2016; Oh et al., 2016; Tuncdemir et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bloodgood et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2015; Marques-Smith et al., 2016; Oh et al., 2016; Tuncdemir et al., 2016.

claim: PV-INs regulate critical-period experience-dependent plasticity.
source: There is also clear evidence suggesting that PV-INs regulate critical-period experience-dependent plasticity (Hensch, 2005; Krishnan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hensch, 2005; Krishnan et al., 2015.

claim: Approximately 5.2% of tdTomato+ neurons in Sst-tdTomato mice expressed PV.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Hu et al., 2013; Pfeffer et al., 2013), we observed that ~5.2% of tdTomato+ neurons expressed PV (5.2 ± 0.3%, nine slices from three mice, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, and citations to Hu et al., 2013; Pfeffer et al., 2013.

claim: Approximately 17.2% of tdTomato+ neurons showed FS properties.
source: Meanwhile, ~17.2% of tdTomato+ neurons showed the FS properties (36 out of 209, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) (Hu et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, and citations to Hu et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2015.

claim: FS tdTomato+ cells exhibited the distinctive basket cell morphology.
source: Furthermore, FS tdTomato+ cells exhibited the distinctive basket cell morphology (4 out of 4, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological reconstruction data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Non-FS tdTomato+ cells were characterized by morphological properties including ascending axonal arborizations with extensive branching in layer one and horizontal collaterals, consistent with Martinotti cells.
source: Non-FS tdTomato+ cells were further characterized by morphological properties, including ascending axonal arborizations with extensive branching in layer one and horizontal collaterals (19 out of 20, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), consistent with those of Martinotti cells as previously described (Fino and Yuste, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological reconstruction data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and a citation to Fino and Yuste, 2011.

claim: Sst-IN→PC connections emerged at postnatal day 7-8 (P7-8).
source: We found that Sst-IN→PC connections emerged at postnatal day 7–8 (P7–8).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from paired recordings at different developmental stages.

claim: The connection probability of Sst-IN→PC synapses increased significantly from P7-8 to P9-11.
source: The connection probability increased significantly from P7–8 to P9–11 (χ2 test, p=0.0046; Figure 1E) and remained largely comparable from P9 to P20 (χ2 test, p=0.149; Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E with statistical analysis (χ2 test, p=0.0046).

claim: The connection probability of Sst-IN→PC synapses remained largely comparable from P9 to P20.
source: The connection probability increased significantly from P7–8 to P9–11 (χ2 test, p=0.0046; Figure 1E) and remained largely comparable from P9 to P20 (χ2 test, p=0.149; Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E with statistical analysis (χ2 test, p=0.149).

claim: There was a ~65% reduction in the peak amplitude of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs from P12-13 to P14-15.
source: Interestingly, we observed a ~65% reduction in the peak amplitude of uIPSCs from P12–13 to P14–15 (P7–8, 17.9 ± 2.9 pA; P9–11, 28.3 ± 5.4 pA; P12–13, 34.3 ± 4.8 pA; P14–15, 11.6 ± 1.8 pA; P16–17, 10.0 ± 1.4 pA; P18–20, 6.0 ± 1.9 pA; one-way ANOVA, F(5,185) = 8.788, p=1.7 × 10−7; Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F with statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA, F(5,185) = 8.788, p=1.7 × 10−7).

claim: The dramatic change in Sst-IN→PC uIPSC amplitude coincided with the natural eye opening of mice under standard living conditions.
source: Notably, this dramatic change coincided with the natural eye opening of mice under standard living conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the weakening of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs may result from eye opening.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the timing of eye opening in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and the timing of uIPSC amplitude changes in Figure 1F.

claim: The 10-90% rise time of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs at P18-20 was significantly longer than that at P7-8 and P12-13.
source: Although the 10–90% rise time of uIPSCs at P18–20 was significantly longer than that at P7–8 and P12–13, the 10–90% rise time of uIPSCs did not significantly change at P9–17 (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The 10-90% rise time of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs did not significantly change at P9-17.
source: Although the 10–90% rise time of uIPSCs at P18–20 was significantly longer than that at P7–8 and P12–13, the 10–90% rise time of uIPSCs did not significantly change at P9–17 (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The half-width of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs did not show any obvious change at P7-20.
source: Furthermore, the half-width of uIPSCs did not show any obvious change at P7–20 (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The total length and complexity of both apical and basal dendrites of PCs exhibited no significant difference between P12-13 and P14-15 mice.
source: In addition, the total length and complexity of both apical and basal dendrites of PCs exhibited no significant difference between P12–13 and P14–15 mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–I), suggesting that dendritic morphology of PCs remains unchanged during eye opening.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B-I.

claim: The connection probability and strength of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission exhibited similar development properties when using cesium-based and high Cl- internal solution to record the postsynaptic currents.
source: Of note, the connection probability and strength of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission exhibited similar development properties when we used cesium-based and high Cl- internal solution to record the postsynaptic currents (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The peak amplitude of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs at P14-15 was significantly smaller than that at P12-13 in the prefrontal Cg1/2 area.
source: Consistent with the result observed in the visual cortex, the peak amplitude of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs at P14–15 was significantly smaller than that at P12–13 in Cg1/2 (P9–11, 31.6 ± 6.6 pA; P12–13, 31.0 ± 4.7 pA; P14–15, 11.0 ± 3.1 pA; P16–17, 5.0 ± 1.9 pA; P18–20, 5.7 ± 1.0 pA; one-way ANOVA, F(4,46) = 5.51, p=6.0 × 10−4; Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C with statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA, F(4,46) = 5.51, p=6.0 × 10−4).

claim: The connection probability of Sst-IN→PC synapses in Cg1/2 remained comparable from P9 to P20.
source: The connection probability remained comparable from P9 to P20 (χ2 test, p=0.857; Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B with statistical analysis (χ2 test, p=0.857).

claim: The weakening of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission during eye opening exists not only in the visual cortex but also in Cg1/2.
source: These results suggest that the weakening of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission during eye opening exists not only in the visual cortex but also in Cg1/2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from both visual cortex (Figure 1) and Cg1/2 (Figure 2) showing similar developmental changes.

claim: 78.4% of recorded EGFP+/tdTomato- cells were FS-INs at P12-18 in Sst-tdTomato::Lhx6-EGFP mice.
source: We found that 78.4% of recorded EGFP+/tdTomato- cells were FS-INs at P12–18 (87 out of 111, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and these FS-INs showed basket cell morphology (15 out of 15, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: FS-INs in Sst-tdTomato::Lhx6-EGFP mice showed basket cell morphology.
source: We found that 78.4% of recorded EGFP+/tdTomato- cells were FS-INs at P12–18 (87 out of 111, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and these FS-INs showed basket cell morphology (15 out of 15, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological reconstruction data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The connection probability of FS-IN→PC synapses did not significantly change from P12 to P18.
source: The connection probability did not significantly change from P12 to P18 (χ2 test, p=0.949; Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D with statistical analysis (χ2 test, p=0.949).

claim: The strength of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs at P14-15 and P16-18 was significantly stronger than that at P12-13.
source: Interestingly, unlike Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission, the strength of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs at P14–15 and P16–18 was significantly stronger than that at P12–13 (P12–13, 91 ± 14 pA; P14–15, 217 ± 37 pA; P16–18, 279 ± 57 pA; one-way ANOVA, F(2,63) = 8.71, p=4.6 × 10−4; Figure 3E), suggesting that eye opening may increase the FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E with statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA, F(2,63) = 8.71, p=4.6 × 10−4).

claim: The 10-90% rise time and half-width of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs did not exhibit obvious change between P12-13 and P14-15.
source: Moreover, the 10–90% rise time and half-width of uIPSCs did not exhibit obvious change between P12–13 and P14–15, while the rise time was significantly shorter at P16–18 than at P12–13 (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: The 10-90% rise time of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs was significantly shorter at P16-18 than at P12-13.
source: Moreover, the 10–90% rise time and half-width of uIPSCs did not exhibit obvious change between P12–13 and P14–15, while the rise time was significantly shorter at P16–18 than at P12–13 (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The peak amplitude of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs at P14-15 and P17-20 was significantly larger than that at P12-13 in Cg1/2 area.
source: In Cg1/2 area, we also observed a significantly larger peak amplitude of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs at P14–15 and P17–20 than that at P12–13 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), while the connection probability was comparable among the three groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The connection probability of FS-IN→PC synapses in Cg1/2 was comparable among P12-13, P14-15, and P17-20 groups.
source: In Cg1/2 area, we also observed a significantly larger peak amplitude of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs at P14–15 and P17–20 than that at P12–13 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), while the connection probability was comparable among the three groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Sst-IN→FS-IN connection probability did not change from P12 to P18.
source: Our data showed that the Sst-IN→FS-IN connection probability did not change from P12 to P18 (χ2 test, p=0.855; Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B with statistical analysis (χ2 test, p=0.855).

claim: The strength of Sst-IN→FS-IN uIPSCs did not exhibit any obvious change from P12 to P18.
source: Notably, the strength of Sst-IN→FS-IN uIPSCs did not exhibit any obvious change (P12–13, 62.0 ± 12.7 pA; P14–15, 72.1 ± 18.7 pA; P16–18, 56.6 ± 13.0 pA; one-way ANOVA, F(2,24) = 0.268, p=0.767, Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C with statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA, F(2,24) = 0.268, p=0.767).

claim: Htr3a-INs are the predominant type of INs in the superficial visual layers, comprising ~50% of layer 2/3 INs.
source: Htr3a-INs are the predominant type of INs in the superficial visual layers, comprising ~50% of layer 2/3 INs (Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2010.

claim: 5HT3a receptors in the neocortex are present exclusively in GABAergic INs.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that 5HT3a receptors (encoded by Htr3a) in the neocortex are present exclusively in GABAergic INs (Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2010.

claim: Only ~1% of tdTomato+ Sst-INs expressed EGFP in Sst-tdTomato::Htr3a-EGFP mice.
source: Only ~1% of tdTomato+ Sst-INs expressed EGFP (1.1 ± 0.7%, six slices from three mice), suggesting that Sst-INs and Htr3a-INs are two different types of INs as previously reported (Chittajallu et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry and citations to Chittajallu et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2010.

claim: Sst-IN→Htr3a-IN connections emerged at P9-11.
source: Sst-IN→Htr3a-IN connections emerged at P9–11, and the probability of connections did not change significantly from P9 to P17 (χ2 test, p=0.169; Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The probability of Sst-IN→Htr3a-IN connections did not change significantly from P9 to P17.
source: Sst-IN→Htr3a-IN connections emerged at P9–11, and the probability of connections did not change significantly from P9 to P17 (χ2 test, p=0.169; Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G with statistical analysis (χ2 test, p=0.169).

claim: There was no obvious difference in the strength of Sst-IN→Htr3a-IN uIPSCs between P12-13 and P14-15 mice.
source: Similar to Sst-IN→FS-IN uIPSCs, there was no obvious difference in the strength of Sst-IN→Htr3a-IN uIPSCs between P12–13 (before eye opening) and P14–15 (after eye opening) mice (P9–11, 19.1 ± 6.8 pA; P12–13, 21.9 ± 7.4 pA; P14–15, 25.6 ± 8.5 pA; P16–17, 28.6 ± 9.9 pA; one-way ANOVA, F(3,37) = 0.183, p=0.907; Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H with statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA, F(3,37) = 0.183, p=0.907).

claim: The connection probability and strength of FS-IN→FS-IN uIPSCs exhibited no significant difference among P12-13, P14-15, and P16-19 groups.
source: Moreover, we found that the connection probability and strength of FS-IN→FS-IN uIPSCs exhibited no significant difference among P12–13, P14–15, and P16–19 groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sst-IN inhibition onto PCs and FS-INs exhibited no significant difference at P12-13.
source: Sst-IN inhibition onto PCs and FS-INs exhibited no significant difference at P12–13 (paired t-test, p=0.510; Figure 5BC and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from triple recordings shown in Figure 5B, C, and E with statistical analysis (paired t-test, p=0.510).

claim: At P14-15, the same Sst-INs produced much larger uIPSCs in FS-INs than in PCs.
source: However, at P14–15, the same Sst-INs produced much larger uIPSCs in FS-INs than in PCs (paired t-test, p=0.037; Figures 5B, D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from triple recordings shown in Figure 5B, D, and E with statistical analysis (paired t-test, p=0.037).

claim: Sst-IN inhibition onto PCs versus that onto Htr3a-INs was not significantly different at P12-13.
source: Similarly, Sst-IN inhibition onto PCs versus that onto Htr3a-INs was not significantly different at P12–13 (paired t-test, p=0.601; Figure 5G and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from triple recordings shown in Figure 5G and I with statistical analysis (paired t-test, p=0.601).

claim: Sst-INs produced significantly larger uIPSCs in layer 2/3 Htr3a-INs than in PCs at P14-15.
source: However, Sst-INs produced significantly larger uIPSCs in layer 2/3 Htr3a-INs than in PCs at P14–15 (paired t-test, p=0.037; Figure 5H and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from triple recordings shown in Figure 5H and I with statistical analysis (paired t-test, p=0.037).

claim: Under dark rearing condition, no significant changes were observed in connection probability of Sst-IN→PC synapses between P12-13 and P14-15.
source: Under dark rearing condition, no significant changes were observed in connection probability (χ2 test, p=0.066; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) nor unitary strength of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission between P12–13 and P14–15 (P12–13, 19.6 ± 4.1 pA, n = 13; P14–15, 21.7 ± 3.6 pA, n = 16; two-tailed unpaired t-test, p=0.702; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from dark-reared mice shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C with statistical analysis (χ2 test, p=0.066).

claim: Under dark rearing condition, no significant changes were observed in unitary strength of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission between P12-13 and P14-15.
source: Under dark rearing condition, no significant changes were observed in connection probability (χ2 test, p=0.066; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) nor unitary strength of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission between P12–13 and P14–15 (P12–13, 19.6 ± 4.1 pA, n = 13; P14–15, 21.7 ± 3.6 pA, n = 16; two-tailed unpaired t-test, p=0.702; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from dark-reared mice shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and D with statistical analysis (two-tailed unpaired t-test, p=0.702).

claim: Visual deprivation prevents the weakening of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission at the time of eye opening.
source: These results suggest that visual deprivation prevents the weakening of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission at the time of eye opening.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing no change in Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission in dark-reared mice.

claim: The connection probability of Sst-IN→PC synapses in visual cortex was not significantly different among continuously sutured mice at P12-13, P14-15, P17-20 and those with eyelids artificially opened at P17-20.
source: For Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission within the visual cortex (VC), the connection probability was not significantly different among the different groups (χ2 test, p=0.958; Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B with statistical analysis (χ2 test, p=0.958).

claim: There was no significant change in the peak amplitude of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs in continuously sutured mice between P12-13 and P14-15.
source: Consistent with dark rearing, there was no significant change in the peak amplitude of uIPSCs in continuously sutured mice between P12–13 and P14–15 (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In continuously sutured mice, the strength of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs at P17-20 was comparable to that at P12-13 or P14-15.
source: Moreover, in continuously sutured mice, the strength of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs at P17–20 was comparable to that at P12–13 or P14–15 (P12–13, 30.1 ± 5.9 pA; P14–15, 25.2 ± 4.1 pA; P17–20, 17.5 ± 10.6 pA; Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The strength of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs at P17-20 in mice with eyelids artificially opened was significantly lower than that in continuously sutured mice at P12-13, P14-15, and P17-20 in visual cortex.
source: Interestingly, the strength of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs at P17–20 in mice with eyelids artificially opened was significantly lower than that in continuously sutured mice at P12–13, P14–15, and P17–20 (one-way ANOVA, F(3,68) = 4.231, p=0.008; Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C with statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA, F(3,68) = 4.231, p=0.008).

claim: Artificial eye opening can induce the weakening of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission.
source: These results suggest that artificial eye opening can induce the weakening of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission and that this change associated with eye opening is unlikely due to an intrinsic developmental program.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that artificially opening the eyes in sutured mice reproduces the weakening of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission.

claim: The change in Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission associated with eye opening is unlikely due to an intrinsic developmental program.
source: These results suggest that artificial eye opening can induce the weakening of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission and that this change associated with eye opening is unlikely due to an intrinsic developmental program.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that the change can be prevented by lid suture and reproduced by artificial eye opening.

claim: The probability of Sst-IN→PC connections in Cg1/2 was not significantly changed among continuously sutured mice at P12-13, P14-15, P17-20 and those with eyelids artificially opened at P17-20.
source: In Cg1/2, the probability of Sst-IN→PC connections was not significantly changed among different groups (χ2 test, p=0.987; Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D with statistical analysis (χ2 test, p=0.987).

claim: The strength of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs remained unchanged in continuously sutured mice at P12-13, P14-15, and P17-20 in Cg1/2.
source: The strength of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs remained unchanged in continuously sutured mice at P12–13, P14–15, and P17–20 (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The strength of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs at P17-20 in mice with eyelids artificially opened was significantly smaller than that in continuously sutured mice at P12-13, P14-15, and P17-20 in Cg1/2.
source: Furthermore, the strength of Sst-IN→PC uIPSCs at P17–20 in mice with eyelids artificially opened was significantly smaller than that in continuously sutured mice at P12–13, P14–15, and P17–20 (artificially eye-opened mice: P17–20, 13.6 ± 2.6 pA versus continuously sutured mice: P12–13, 37.3 ± 5.7 pA; P14–15, 54.6 ± 14.7 pA; and P17–20, 39.9 ± 8.3 pA; one-way ANOVA, F(3,39) = 5.607, p=0.003; Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E with statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA, F(3,39) = 5.607, p=0.003).

claim: Both the connection probability and strength of Sst-IN→FS-IN synaptic transmission were comparable at P12-13 and P14-15 in continuously sutured mice.
source: In addition, both the connection probability and strength of Sst-IN→FS-IN synaptic transmission were comparable at P12–13 and P14–15 in continuously sutured mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: There were no significant changes in the connection probability of FS-IN→PC synapses in visual cortex among continuously sutured mice at P12-13, P14-15, P17-20 and those with eyelids artificially opened at P17-20.
source: For FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission in VC, similar to Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission, there were no significant changes in the connection probability among the different groups (χ2 test, p=0.722; Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F with statistical analysis (χ2 test, p=0.722).

claim: The strength of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs was similar in continuously sutured mice at P12-13, P14-15, and P17-20.
source: Similarly, the strength of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs was similar in continuously sutured mice at P12–13, P14–15, and P17–20.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The strength of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs in artificially eye-opened mice at P17-20 was significantly stronger than that in continuously sutured mice at P12-13, P14-15, and P17-20 in visual cortex.
source: In contrast, the strength in artificially eye-opened mice at P17–20 was significantly stronger than that in continuously sutured mice at P12–13, P14–15, and P17–20 (artificially eye-opened mice: P17–20, 241 ± 39 pA versus continuously sutured mice: P12–13, 84 ± 25 pA; P14–15, 98 ± 21 pA; and P17–20, 108 ± 19 pA; one-way ANOVA, F(3,75) = 7.096, p=2.9 × 10−4; Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G with statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA, F(3,75) = 7.096, p=2.9 × 10−4).

claim: The strength of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs in continuously sutured mice at P12-13, P14-15, and P17-20 was comparable in Cg1/2 area.
source: In the Cg1/2 area, although the strength of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs in continuously sutured mice at P12–13, P14–15, and P17–20 was comparable, the strength in artificially eye-opened mice at P17–20 was also significantly stronger than that in continuously sutured mice at P12–13, P14–15, and P17–20 (Figure 6I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The strength of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs in artificially eye-opened mice at P17-20 was significantly stronger than that in continuously sutured mice at P12-13, P14-15, and P17-20 in Cg1/2 area.
source: In the Cg1/2 area, although the strength of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs in continuously sutured mice at P12–13, P14–15, and P17–20 was comparable, the strength in artificially eye-opened mice at P17–20 was also significantly stronger than that in continuously sutured mice at P12–13, P14–15, and P17–20 (Figure 6I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: No significant changes in the connection probability of FS-IN→PC synapses were observed among different groups in Cg1/2 area.
source: Furthermore, no significant changes in the connection probability were observed among the different groups (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Both the connection probability and strength of FS-IN→FS-IN synaptic transmission were comparable at P12-13 and P14-15 in continuously sutured mice.
source: In addition, both the connection probability and strength of FS-IN→FS-IN synaptic transmission were comparable at P12–13 and P14–15 in continuously sutured mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: There were no significant differences in PPR, C.V., or failure rate in Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission before and after eye opening at P12-13 and at P14-15.
source: In Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission, there were no significant differences in PPR (two-way ANOVA, F(2,132) = 0.172, p=0.842; Figure 7A and Figure 7B), C.V. (P12–13, 0.494 ± 0.052, n = 20; P14–15, 0.472 ± 0.052, n = 23; two-tailed unpaired t-test, p=0.775; Figure 7C), or failure rate (P12–13, 4.8 ± 2.2%, n = 20; P14–15, 5.3 ± 2.8%, n = 23; two-tailed unpaired t-test, p=0.897; Figure 7D) before and after eye opening at P12–13 and at P14–15.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-D with statistical analyses.

claim: Eye opening does not affect the presynaptic release probability in Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission.
source: These results suggest that eye opening does not affect the presynaptic release probability in Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing no changes in PPR, C.V., or failure rate.

claim: The number of presynaptic release sites (N) in Sst-IN→PC connections at P12-13 was similar to that at P14-15.
source: We found that N in presynaptic terminals at P12–13 was similar to that at P14–15 (P12–13, 12.3 ± 1.5, n = 12; P14–15, 14.3 ± 1.9, n = 8; two-tailed unpaired t-test, p=0.419, Figure 7G).
evidence: The claim is supported by variance-mean analysis data shown in Figure 7G with statistical analysis (two-tailed unpaired t-test, p=0.419).

claim: The postsynaptic quantal size (Q) in Sst-IN→PC connections at P14-15 was significantly lower than that at P12-13.
source: However, Q at P14–15 was significantly lower than that at P12–13 (P12–13, 20.2 ± 2.2 pA, n = 12; P14–15, 8.7 ± 0.9 pA, n = 8; Mann Whitney U test, p=2.9 × 10−4; Figure 7H), suggesting that postsynaptic mechanisms contribute to the developmental weakening of Sst-IN→PC synaptic strength.
evidence: The claim is supported by variance-mean analysis data shown in Figure 7H with statistical analysis (Mann Whitney U test, p=2.9 × 10−4).

claim: Postsynaptic mechanisms contribute to the developmental weakening of Sst-IN→PC synaptic strength.
source: However, Q at P14–15 was significantly lower than that at P12–13 (P12–13, 20.2 ± 2.2 pA, n = 12; P14–15, 8.7 ± 0.9 pA, n = 8; Mann Whitney U test, p=2.9 × 10−4; Figure 7H), suggesting that postsynaptic mechanisms contribute to the developmental weakening of Sst-IN→PC synaptic strength.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing a significant decrease in postsynaptic quantal size without changes in presynaptic release probability or number of release sites.

claim: There were no significant differences in PPR, C.V., or failure rate in FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission between P12-13 and P14-15 mice.
source: Similarly, in FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission, there were no significant differences in PPR, C.V., or failure rate between P12–13 and P14–15 mice (Figures 7I, J, K and L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7I, J, K and L.

claim: The average values of N in FS-IN→PC connections at P12-13 and P14-15 were not significantly different.
source: Moreover, the average values of N at P12–13 and P14–15 were not significantly different (P12–13, 12.9 ± 3.1, n = 8; P14–15, 15.8 ± 1.9, n = 8; two-tailed unpaired t-test, p=0.439, Figure 7O).
evidence: The claim is supported by variance-mean analysis data shown in Figure 7O with statistical analysis (two-tailed unpaired t-test, p=0.439).

claim: The postsynaptic quantal size (Q) of FS-IN→PC connections at P14-15 was significantly larger than that at P12-13.
source: Unlike Sst-IN→PC connections, Q of FS-IN→PC connections at P14–15 was significantly larger than that at P12–13 (P12–13, 11.5 ± 1.9 pA, n = 8; P14–15, 27.5 ± 6.2 pA, n = 8; two-tailed unpaired t-test, p=0.026, Figure 7P).
evidence: The claim is supported by variance-mean analysis data shown in Figure 7P with statistical analysis (two-tailed unpaired t-test, p=0.026).

claim: The postsynaptic quantal sizes in both Sst-IN→PC and FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission are altered during eye opening.
source: Together, these results suggest the postsynaptic quantal sizes in both of Sst-IN→PC and FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission are altered during eye opening.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing changes in postsynaptic quantal size in both types of connections.

claim: Eye opening weakens the synaptic transmission from Sst-INs to PCs.
source: In this study, we show the following: (1) eye opening weakens the synaptic transmission from Sst-INs to PCs, but increases the synaptic transmission from FS-INs to PCs
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing decreased Sst-IN→PC uIPSC amplitude during eye opening.

claim: Eye opening increases the synaptic transmission from FS-INs to PCs.
source: In this study, we show the following: (1) eye opening weakens the synaptic transmission from Sst-INs to PCs, but increases the synaptic transmission from FS-INs to PCs
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing increased FS-IN→PC uIPSC amplitude during eye opening.

claim: The inhibitory synaptic transmission from Sst-INs to other types of interneurons remains unaltered during eye opening.
source: (2) the inhibitory synaptic transmission from Sst-INs to other types of interneurons remains unaltered during eye opening
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no changes in Sst-IN→FS-IN and Sst-IN→Htr3a-IN synaptic transmission during eye opening.

claim: Eye opening-induced alteration of the inhibitory synaptic transmission onto PCs is mediated by changes in postsynaptic quantal size.
source: (3) eye opening-induced alteration of the inhibitory synaptic transmission onto PCs is mediated by changes in postsynaptic quantal size.
evidence: The claim is supported by variance-mean analysis data showing changes in postsynaptic quantal size without changes in presynaptic parameters.

claim: The plasticity of GABAergic circuitry in the visual critical period in the developing visual cortex has been extensively studied by manipulations that disrupt normal visual experience after eye opening.
source: The plasticity of GABAergic circuitry in the visual critical period in the developing visual cortex has been extensively studied by manipulations that disrupt normal visual experience after eye opening (Griffen and Maffei, 2014; Hensch, 2005; Lefort et al., 2013; Maffei et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Griffen and Maffei, 2014; Hensch, 2005; Lefort et al., 2013; Maffei et al., 2004.

claim: The changes and plasticity of GABAergic circuitry during eye opening are still far from fully understood.
source: However, the changes and plasticity of GABAergic circuitry during eye opening are still far from fully understood (Gandhi et al., 2005; Kuhlman et al., 2011; Maffei et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gandhi et al., 2005; Kuhlman et al., 2011; Maffei et al., 2004.

claim: The average probability of Sst-IN→PC connections is ~58% within 100 µm at P12-20.
source: The average probability of Sst-IN→PC connections (~58% within 100 µm at P12–20) observed in this study agreed with that obtained via paired recordings in layer 2/3 of the somatosensory cortex (~63%) (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from paired recordings and a citation to Xu et al., 2013.

claim: Connection strength from low-threshold spiking interneurons to excitatory spinal neurons increases from P12-13 to P14-15 in layer 4 of the rat somatosensory cortex.
source: Although the developmental synaptic transmission from Sst-INs onto PCs has not been quantified systematically, previous work reported that connection strength from low-threshold spiking interneurons (putative Sst-INs) to excitatory spinal neurons increases from P12–13 to P14–15 in layer 4 of the rat somatosensory cortex (Long et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Long et al., 2005.

claim: Both the connection probability and strength of Sst-IN→PC synaptic connections decrease substantially from P14-15 to P20-22 within layer 4 of the mouse visual cortex.
source: In contrast, a recent study found that both the connection probability and strength of Sst-IN→PC synaptic connections decrease substantially from P14–15 to P20–22 within layer 4 of the mouse visual cortex (Miao et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Miao et al., 2016.

claim: FS-IN→PC unitary conductance remains unaltered after P8 in layer 5/6 of mouse visual cortex.
source: However, FS-IN→PC unitary conductance was reported to remain unaltered after P8 in layer 5/6 of mouse visual cortex (Pangratz-Fuehrer and Hestrin, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pangratz-Fuehrer and Hestrin, 2011.

claim: The strength of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs is not changed after P9 in layer 5/6 of mouse prefrontal cortex.
source: Similarly, Yang et al. observed that the strength of FS-IN→PC uIPSCs is not changed after P9 in layer 5/6 of mouse prefrontal cortex (Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2014.

claim: FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission does not change in the cortical layer 5/6 during eye opening.
source: These studies imply that FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission does not change in the cortical layer 5/6 during eye opening.
evidence: The claim is inferred from citations to studies showing no changes in FS-IN→PC synaptic transmission after P8-P9 in layer 5/6.

claim: Eye opening has been shown to affect hippocampal development.
source: Indeed, eye opening has been shown to affect hippocampal development, and early eye opening accelerated the maturation of synaptic strength (Dumas, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dumas, 2004.

claim: Early eye opening accelerated the maturation of synaptic strength in the hippocampus.
source: Indeed, eye opening has been shown to affect hippocampal development, and early eye opening accelerated the maturation of synaptic strength (Dumas, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dumas, 2004.

claim: Although the synaptic strength of Sst-IN→PC connection significantly decreases from P14-15 to P20-22 within layer 4 of the mouse visual cortex, dark rearing does not affect the weakening of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission.
source: Of note, a recent study found that although the synaptic strength of Sst-IN→PC connection significantly decreases from P14–15 to P20–22 within layer 4 of the mouse visual cortex, dark rearing does not affect the weakening of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission (Miao et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Miao et al., 2016.

claim: Brief monocular visual deprivation during the time of eye opening selectively reduces the strength of synaptic transmission from PV-INs to PCs in layer 4 of the visual cortex.
source: Moreover, it has been reported that brief monocular visual deprivation during the time of eye opening selectively reduces the strength of synaptic transmission from PV-INs to PCs in layer 4 of the visual cortex (Maffei et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maffei et al., 2004.

claim: Visual deprivation-induced change in GABAergic circuits is layer- and cell type-specific.
source: These results suggest that visual deprivation-induced change in GABAergic circuits is layer- and cell type-specific.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparisons of different studies showing different effects of visual deprivation in different layers and cell types.

claim: There are striking differences in morphology, intrinsic electrophysiological properties, and synaptic connectivity between layer 2/3 and layer 4 Sst-INs.
source: Indeed, accumulating evidence suggests that there are striking differences in morphology, intrinsic electrophysiological properties, and synaptic connectivity between layer 2/3 and layer 4 Sst-INs (Ma et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ma et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2013.

claim: Htr3a-INs encompass a heterogeneous population of INs, including Vip-INs, Npy-INs, and other types of INs.
source: It should be noted that Htr3a-INs encompass a heterogeneous population of INs, including Vip-INs, Npy-INs, and other types of INs (Chittajallu et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2010; Pfeffer et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chittajallu et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2010; Pfeffer et al., 2013.

claim: GABAA receptors mediate the majority of inhibitory synaptic transmission in the mammalian cortex.
source: It is well known that GABAA receptors (including different subunits) mediate the majority of inhibitory synaptic transmission in the mammalian cortex (Bowery and Smart, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bowery and Smart, 2006 and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: Different subunits of GABAA receptor are selectively inserted at specific GABAergic synapses.
source: In addition, different subunits of GABAA receptor are selectively inserted at specific GABAergic synapses (Ali and Thomson, 2008; Nusser et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ali and Thomson, 2008; Nusser et al., 1996.

claim: The expression of GABAA receptor subunits in neocortex changes significantly during early postnatal development.
source: Moreover, previous studies indicated that the expression of GABAA receptor subunits in neocortex changes significantly during early postnatal development (Bowery and Smart, 2006; Fritschy et al., 1994; Heinen et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bowery and Smart, 2006; Fritschy et al., 1994; Heinen et al., 2004.

claim: The changes in subunit expression and/or composition of the GABAA receptor may induce the differential developmental alternations of Sst-IN→PC and FS-IN→PC synaptic strength during eye opening.
source: These findings suggest that the changes in subunit expression and/or composition of the GABAA receptor may induce the differential developmental alternations of Sst-IN→PC and FS-IN→PC synaptic strength during eye opening.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from known changes in GABAA receptor expression during development.

claim: Sst-INs that densely innervate nearby PC dendrites in mouse cortical layer 2/3 are responsible for controlling the efﬁcacy and plasticity of synaptic inputs.
source: Growing evidence suggests that Sst-INs that densely innervate nearby PC dendrites in mouse cortical layer 2/3 are responsible for controlling the efﬁcacy and plasticity of synaptic inputs (Chen et al., 2015; Chiu et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2015; Chiu et al., 2013.

claim: In early postnatal life, GABAergic transmission is excitatory to immature postsynaptic neurons.
source: Given that in early postnatal life, GABAergic transmission is excitatory to immature postsynaptic neurons (Ben-Ari, 2002; Owens et al., 1996), early emergence of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission may enhance the excitability of PCs, thereby promoting their maturation and synaptogenesis (Oh et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ben-Ari, 2002; Owens et al., 1996.

claim: Early emergence of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission may enhance the excitability of PCs, thereby promoting their maturation and synaptogenesis.
source: Given that in early postnatal life, GABAergic transmission is excitatory to immature postsynaptic neurons (Ben-Ari, 2002; Owens et al., 1996), early emergence of Sst-IN→PC synaptic transmission may enhance the excitability of PCs, thereby promoting their maturation and synaptogenesis (Oh et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the excitatory nature of early GABAergic transmission and a citation to Oh et al., 2016.

claim: Around the time of eye opening, Sst-INs would inhibit PCs.
source: However, around the time of eye opening, Sst-INs would inhibit PCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the known developmental switch in GABAergic transmission from excitatory to inhibitory.

claim: Decreased Sst-IN→PC inhibition after eye opening could enhance the effect of visual input onto excitatory neurons in the visual cortex by facilitating dendritic events in distal regions.
source: Therefore, decreased Sst-IN→PC inhibition after eye opening could enhance the effect of visual input onto excitatory neurons in the visual cortex by facilitating dendritic events in distal regions (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observed decrease in Sst-IN→PC inhibition and the known role of Sst-INs in regulating dendritic events.

claim: FS-INs control the spike output of PCs by inhibiting their perisomatic sites.
source: Contrary to Sst-INs, FS-INs control the spike output of PCs by inhibiting their perisomatic sites.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the anatomical and functional properties of FS-INs.

claim: Increased FS-IN→PC inhibition after eye opening is a homeostatic response to the reduction of Sst-IN inhibition and the resulting increase in the excitability of PCs.
source: Increased FS-IN→PC inhibition after eye opening is a homeostatic response to the reduction of Sst-IN inhibition and the resulting increase in the excitability of PCs (Bloodgood et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observed changes in inhibitory transmission and citations to Bloodgood et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2015.

claim: Enhanced visual input to the visual cortex gated by Sst-INs and the homeostatic rebalancing of inhibition regulated by FS-INs might be important for visual integration, an essential step in visual perception.
source: We speculate that such enhanced visual input to the visual cortex gated by Sst-INs and the homeostatic rebalancing of inhibition regulated by FS-INs might be important for visual integration, an essential step in visual perception.
evidence: The claim is explicitly speculative, as indicated by the phrase 'We speculate'.

claim: At P14, 77.9% ± 7.4% of mice had opened eyes.
source: At P14, 77.9% ± 7.4% of mice had opened eyes; at P15, 100% of mice had opened eyes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: At P15, 100% of mice had opened eyes.
source: At P14, 77.9% ± 7.4% of mice had opened eyes; at P15, 100% of mice had opened eyes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There were no mice with opened eyes at P13.
source: There were no mice with opened eyes at P13.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.
